full_judgment: 9. Under Article 103(3) of the Constitution the Appellate Division has been vested with the jurisdiction to hear and determine any appeal from judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division in a case to which clause (2) does not apply, only if leave to appeal is granted by this Division except in three cases as spelt out it Article 103(1), (2) and (3) of the Constitution where appeal to this Division is a matter of right. Of course, Parliament has the right to add to the list other cases in which appeal as of right may be filed. The Constitution has not put any limitation on the power of the Appellate Division to grant leave and, as such, granting of leave is completely in the discretion of the Appellate Division which is exercise by this Division on the wisdom and good sense of the judges of the said Division. But leave shall not be granted where the grounds suggested cannot sustain in the appeal itself. Conversely the appeal will not be allowed on grounds that would not have sufficed for the grant of leave. The basic principle followed in granting leave is that there has been some illegality in the decision of the High Court Division or that there had been some miscarriage of justice or that an evil precedent has been or will be created. The main purpose of granting leave is to determine the point on which the Appellate Division is required to answer. Thus the Court does not hear an appeal on a point on which leave has not been granted. Of course, in exceptional circumstances the Court may allow the appellant to raise such a point as has been done in the case of Wajear Rahman vs State, reported in 43 DLR (AD) 25.
